title: Come Out of Her, My People
paragraphs:
Come Out of Her, My People
The Forgotten Cry of Heaven That Still Echoes Through a Broken World
There are moments in Scripture that feel less like words on a page and more like a voice breaking through the noise of human history.
This is one of them.
A voice that does not whisper.
A voice that does not negotiate.
A voice that calls.
A voice that pleads.
A voice that warns.
And somehow, a voice that still loves.
The words appear in the final book of the Bible, surrounded by judgment, collapse, deception, and the downfall of everything humanity once trusted:
"Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, 'Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues.'" (Revelation 18:4)
In the original Greek text, the command begins with the phrase:

Ἐξέλθατε ἐξ αὐτῆς, ὁ λαός μου
(Exelthate ex autēs, ho laos mou)
Literally:
"Come out from her, My people."
Notice something remarkable.
God does not say, "Come out, strangers."
He does not say, "Come out, unbelievers."
He says:
"My people."
The warning is directed toward people who belong to Him.
That alone should stop every reader in their tracks.
Because the greatest danger in Revelation is not merely persecution from outside.
It is compromise from within.
The voice from heaven is calling people who still bear God's name but have become comfortable living among things that are slowly killing their souls.
This is not merely a prophecy about a future city.
It is a revelation of a spiritual reality that has existed throughout human history.
Babylon is more than a location.
Babylon is humanity organized without God.
Babylon is power without righteousness.
Success without holiness.
Religion without repentance.
Pleasure without truth.
Prosperity without obedience.
Babylon began long before Revelation.
Its roots stretch all the way back to Genesis.
After the flood, humanity gathered together in rebellion against God and built the Tower of Babel.
The Hebrew word is:

בָּבֶל
(Bāvel)
From there came confusion, pride, self-exaltation, and human systems built upon independence from the Creator.
The spirit of Babylon has never disappeared.
It simply changes clothes.
Sometimes it wears political clothing.
Sometimes religious clothing.
Sometimes entertainment clothing.
Sometimes cultural clothing.
Sometimes it wears our own ambitions.
Sometimes it even hides inside our hearts.
That is why Revelation's warning remains so relevant.
Many people assume "Come out of her" means physically separating from the world.
But Jesus Himself prayed something different.
In John 17:15 He said:
"I do not ask that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one."
Christ never called His followers to isolation.
He called them to holiness.
The Greek word for holy is:

ἅγιος
(hagios)
Meaning:
"Set apart."
Not absent from the world.
Set apart within it.
A ship belongs in the water.
The danger comes when the water gets inside the ship.
Likewise, Christians live in the world.
The danger begins when the spirit of the world begins living inside the Christian.
That is the deeper meaning of Revelation 18:4.
God is calling His people out of spiritual compromise.
Out of divided loyalties.
Out of hidden sins.
Out of comfortable hypocrisy.
Out of counterfeit Christianity.
Out of anything that competes with Christ.
Because God has never wanted partial surrender.
The greatest scandals in Scripture were not merely moral failures.
They were stories of divided hearts.
David committed adultery and murder.
Peter denied Christ.
The Samaritan woman had five husbands.
The thief on the cross lived a criminal life.
Mary Magdalene carried a painful past.
Yet Jesus rewrote every one of their stories.
Why?
Because grace is greater than scandal.
That is the entire message of the Gospel.
The enemy says your failures define you.
Jesus says your repentance can redefine you.
The enemy says your past is permanent.
Jesus says redemption creates a new future.
The enemy points to what you've done.
Jesus points to what He has done.
This is why the command to come out of Babylon is ultimately not about fear.
It is about invitation.
The voice calling people out is the same voice that once called Lazarus out of a tomb.
The same voice that called fishermen away from empty nets.
The same voice that called tax collectors away from greed.
The same voice that called sinners into forgiveness.
The same voice that still calls people today.
The Hebrew concept behind repentance helps us understand this beautifully.
The word is:

שׁוּב
(Shuv)
Meaning:
"To turn back. To return."
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling bad.
It is coming home.
It is returning to the God who never stopped pursuing you.
Maybe that is why this passage feels so personal.
Because most people know what it feels like to live in Babylon.
Not the ancient city.
The modern version.
The endless pursuit of more.
The exhausting need for approval.
The secret addiction.
The hidden compromise.
The bitterness nobody sees.
The wounds we medicate instead of surrender.
The success that somehow still leaves us empty.
Many readers know exactly what it feels like to gain the world and quietly lose pieces of their soul.
And then one day, through a sermon, a conversation, a crisis, a Bible verse, or even an article like this, they hear a voice again.
"Come out of her, My people."
Come back.
Return.
Come home.
The beauty of the Gospel is that God's call always arrives with God's grace.
Jesus did not come merely to expose Babylon.
He came to rescue people trapped inside it.
The Apostle Paul writes:
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became worthy.
Not after we fixed everything.
While we were still sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
And that is why the cross stands at the center of history.
At Calvary, every human scandal collided with divine mercy.
Every failure met forgiveness.
Every sinner met a Savior.
Every hopeless ending encountered a resurrected beginning.
The Gospel is not a story about good people finding God.
It is a story about God finding broken people.
And rewriting everything.
Maybe you have spent years carrying guilt.
Maybe you feel disqualified.
Maybe you have hidden parts of your life from everyone around you.
Maybe you have convinced yourself that your story is beyond redemption.
If so, hear this clearly:
The call to come out of Babylon is not condemnation.
It is rescue.
It is Jesus standing at the door of your heart and saying:
"There is more for you than this."
More peace.
More freedom.
More purpose.
More grace.
More life.
More of Him.
And perhaps that is why Revelation 18:4 remains one of the most loving warnings in all of Scripture.
Because judgment is coming upon Babylon.
But before judgment falls, grace calls.
Before destruction arrives, mercy invites.
Before the door closes, Jesus still reaches out His hand.
The question is not whether He is calling.
The question is whether we will answer.
If this message stirred something deep inside you, don't keep it to yourself.
"I'm coming home."
Or simply:
"Jesus, rewrite my story."
Your testimony may be the very thing God uses to encourage someone else.
Because every share spreads the Gospel.
Every comment strengthens community.
And every act of faithfulness becomes part of a much bigger story that God is writing.
The voice is still calling.
The door is still open.
Grace is still reaching.
And Jesus is still rewriting lives.
The greatest tragedy is not that Babylon is falling.
The greatest tragedy would be hearing His voice and refusing to leave.
